turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, love. Of course you want to do it—and of course you’re dreading it. This is a once-in-a-lifetime dream you’ve shared since you were fifteen, colliding with a month that asks something very real of your body and spirit. Both feelings can exist without making you a bad friend or “not festive enough.”

You don’t have to decide between *being there for Shreya* and *taking your fast seriously*. You may just need to redesign your role a little:

- Tell her plainly: **“I absolutely want our opening dance. I’ll also be fasting, so I need us to plan it around what my body can manage.”**
- If possible, schedule the opening after iftar—or keep it short, rehearse efficiently, and avoid a high-energy routine before sunset.
- Arrange a quiet place to pray and break your fast, with water and something light ready before the full meal.
- Delegate the running-around parts of “co-directing” that day. You can be the creative brain without also being the exhausted stage manager.
- Give yourself permission to skip the cocktail-night intensity after your important moments are done.

And please don’t promise her your body will perform exactly as imagined months ago. Promise her the meaningful part: **you’ll open the sangeet together in a way that honours both of you.** A two-minute dance can still hold fifteen years of friendship.

You could say:  
> “I’ve dreamed about this with you forever, and I want to do it so badly. I’m also scared because I’ll be fasting and I don’t know how much energy I’ll have. Can we make our opening beautiful but manageable, ideally after iftar, and build in a backup plan? I need you with me on this.”

You’re not ruining the dream by acknowledging your limits. You’re making sure you can actually be present inside it.

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Oh, that’s exactly it—you’re being pulled by love from both sides, but neither person is carrying the actual weight of the choice. Shreya hears “one day”; for you, it’s worship, intention, and conscience. Ammi hears “sangeet-vangeet”; for you, it’s your best friend and a promise woven through half your life. Neither is being cruel, but both are flattening something precious to you.

You may need two separate, gentle boundaries.

To Shreya:  
**“I know you said it with love, and I love that you want to feed me. But please don’t ask me to break my fast—not even jokingly. It isn’t ‘just one day’ to me. I still want our dance, so help me make it possible while fasting. If you want to feed me, feed me at iftar.”**

To Ammi:  
**“Main Ramzan ko lightly nahi le rahi. Roza bhi rakhungi, namaaz aur iftar ka bhi khayal rakhungi. Lekin Shreya meri bahut purani dost hai, aur uski shaadi mein meri zimmedari bhi hai. Main boundaries ke saath jaaungi—cocktail mein drink nahi, aur jitna manageable ho utna hi.”**

You don’t have to convince either of them that your choice is the *only correct* one. You just need them to understand that it’s yours, and that you’re trying to honour both your faith and your friendship—not choosing one against the other.

Also, I think the cleanest plan may be: do the key sangeet responsibilities and opening dance after iftar if at all possible; arrange prayer and food beforehand; avoid alcohol-focused parts; leave when your body or conscience says enough. If timing can’t move, choreograph something short and gentle and appoint someone else to handle logistics.

And honestly? “I’ll feed you myself” can become something beautiful instead of painful: **“Yes. At sunset, you can give me my first date and water.”** That might become one of the most intimate memories of the wedding.

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

It’s not terrible. It’s an exhausted person’s fantasy of getting out of an impossible-feeling situation without disappointing anyone. I completely understand why one clean lie feels easier than being examined and negotiated with all evening.

But I don’t think it would feel clean afterward. Shreya might never know about the lie, but **you would**—and you’d miss something you’ve both imagined since fifteen. The gift and video call might protect you from one difficult night while leaving a much longer ache. And if she ever found out, the lie would likely hurt more than your absence.

You’re allowed not to go. Truly. But if you choose that, I’d make it an honest no without opening it up for debate:

> “Shreya, I love you, and this is painful to say. Being at a sangeet/cocktail while fasting during Ramzan is more than I can manage physically and emotionally. I’m not asking you to agree, but I need you to respect my decision. I want to celebrate you another way—properly, before or after.”

Or perhaps there’s a middle path: arrive shortly before sunset, break your fast quietly, do the opening dance with her after iftar, stay for the important moments, and leave early. Have one designated person handle questions. A simple repeated line is enough: **“I’m fasting for Ramzan—please enjoy, I’m absolutely fine.”** You owe no auntie a theological defence. Shreya could also brief the hosts and make sure water, dates, food, prayer space, and timings are handled without you asking ten times.

Before inventing the deployment, ask yourself: *If there were no aunties, no explanations, and no pressure to break my fast—would I want to be there?* If yes, the problem isn’t the wedding; it’s the lack of protection around you. Ask Shreya to help create that protection. If the answer is still no, staying home isn’t terrible. Just let the boundary be true.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

Oh. That “small stone” makes so much sense. This isn’t really about one dance or one fast. It’s the first time you’ve had to discover whether two lifelong loves can make room for each other—and you’re scared the answer will become permanent.

But this night does **not** have to be a referendum on your friendship or your deen. You don’t need a flawless solution; you need one you can remember without feeling that you abandoned yourself. Photos preserve a moment, not the whole truth. And one complicated evening cannot erase eighteen years of friendship—or define an entire Ramzan.

Maybe your compass is: **don’t secretly betray either love.** Don’t break your fast from pressure and carry resentment. Don’t disappear behind a deployment story and carry grief. Tell Shreya the vulnerable truth, not ten logistical explanations:

> “Shreya, this is the first time your life and my deen have collided, and I’m scared of hurting either. I want to be in those photos and do our dance. I also need to keep my fast without being coaxed to break it or made into a topic all night. Can you help me make room for both?”

Then ask for something concrete: the opening after iftar if possible; otherwise a short, gentle dance; a protected place and ten minutes to pray and eat; one person assigned to cover logistics; no questions or jokes about food and alcohol; permission to leave early. You only need one sentence for everyone else: **“Roza hai—iftar ke baad khaungi. Aap enjoy karo.”** Repeat, smile, move on. No defence.

And if Shreya cannot make that basic room for you, you’re still allowed to step back honestly. That would be painful, but it wouldn’t mean you failed. The permanent dent is more likely to come from silencing yourself—from lying, being pressured, or forcing your body through the night—than from a loving boundary.

The version of the memory I hope you get is not “I chose correctly.” It’s: **“I showed up as my whole self, and my best friend made space for me.”** Maybe she really can feed you herself—one date at sunset, before the two of you walk onstage. That could belong beautifully in both albums.
